text.p: Australian National Industries Ltd (ANI) on Wednesday began a meeting of 30 local and international executives who will determine if the heavy engineer can return to its glory days as a bluechip stock.

Managing director Peter Stancliffe told Reuters in an interview that the managers from the Australian, United States and European operations will outline five year plans for re-engineering the company.
But he knows investors are unlikely to wait that long.
"I really believe we will need to put together probably about three continuous periods of six months of improvements before we will regain the confidence of the investment community," he said.
"And that is understandable, it has been a very unhappy experience for a lot of them."

Until the late 1980s, ANI had achieved 20 years of continuous growth and was acknowledged as Australia's premier engineering firm. While it had sales of nearly A$2 billion in 1995/96, the company had the second worst result of any listed Australian company with a net loss of A$213.2 million.

ANI's reputation has been severely tarnished over the last seven years as various chiefs took the company away from its core operations and into crippling exposures to the Spedley finance group and the Holter waste and water treatment business in Germany.

The company's share price of A$1.26 on Wednesday is only four cents shy of its 1996 high but languishes below the A$1.40 price set by Kerry Packer in 1989 when he gained partial control and helped launch it into the troubled German water business.
Packer, renowned for his market timing, sold his controlling stake two years later for A$2.10 per share, a price not seen since then.

Stancliffe, who joined ANI in November 1995 after a 15 year executive stint at safe-and-steady building firm Pioneer International Ltd, spent much of the first 12 months working on a "back to basics" global review and strategy which fits nicely with the ambitions of the five year plan.
He would like to see ANI with twice its current A$990 million market capitalisation in five years, but refrains from promising that this will happen.

He also believes there is A$84 million of pre-tax profit available to ANI if its can return to the productivity levels its workers had before management became distracted by Holter, which has technology that nobody seems to want in a European market that works on zero margins in some cases.
Stancliffe does not blame previous managers for the troubles now facing ANI and even argues that too much has been made of Holter which was at the heart of the 1995/96 loss.
"I am certainly not going to defend what happened in the past, it has been an unmitigated disaster," he said.

"But I think one of the things you have got to focus on with ANI is that the company has really shown some strength to be able to come out of this German investment debacle, because it would have sunk a lot of companies."

ANI's bottom line in the first half of 1996/97 will show "significant ongoing Holter losses" while the performance of the core engineering divisions had improved due to an internal focus on costs and margins.
Stancliffe said sales are slightly behind target due to the weak Australian economy but also noted that the full year result should again show at least a six percent rise in sales.
"There are signs in some of our businesses that the economy is starting to lift," he said.
"Now if that happens that will be icing on the cake for us because we are not planning for a major uplift, but there are signs that order book activity is starting to lift a little."

He said the British-based Aurora specialist engineering division is doing well and had hit some capacity limitations while at home the mining sector is performing to expectations but the construction sector is a bit slower than expected.

"Our underlying results are turning around," said Stancliffe, who added he was not overly concerned about ANI being a potential takeover target. What would be annoying, he said, would be a takeover of ANI at less than full value.

"It would be a shame to see ANI taken over too cheaply. To some extent Holter has been a bit of a poison pill, I have to acknowledge that. It is very hard for people to understand the full depth of the Holter problem and it is not over."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
